story.title: Naming the scene requires evidence beyond the pixels
paragraphs: A generic caption can say that a person is speaking at a podium; a news caption must say who and at which event, and over 96% of captions in common news datasets contain entities (Tran et al., 2020). Many such facts are not visible, and the article also names people who are not pictured.

Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) rarely produce entities zero-shot and stay weak on them after official fine-tuning. InstructBLIP (7B), whose connector compresses the image into 32 tokens and leaves the most room for article text, performs best of those tested and becomes the backbone. Even so, truncating the article can drop the needed name, while the full article can bury it.

mechanism.title: The auxiliary tasks teach two different kinds of relevance
paragraphs: Entity-Aware Sentence Selection turns caption data into an image–text matching task: article sentences that share a visual entity with the reference caption are positives, and same-article sentences without one are hard negatives, close in topic but differing in entities. Non-visual entities such as dates do not count. Unlike CLIP-style matchers trained on open-domain captions, this adds no separate training stage.

Entity Selection asks the model to list the article's entities that also appear in the caption, including non-visual ones. Labels for both tasks come from SpaCy entity matches against training captions, and both are trained jointly with captioning. At inference the same model extracts sentences and entities, adds them to its usual context within a 600-word limit, and writes the caption.

evidence.title: Selecting entity context beats reading more of the article
paragraphs: On NYTimes800k (Table 2), fully fine-tuning InstructBLIP beats the official connector-only recipe, 82.70 versus 75.95 CIDEr, the caption metric that weights rare words such as names most. Each alignment task helps alone, both together reach 84.45, and self-supplemented generation adds the largest step among EAMA's components. Reading the full article lifts the caption-only model only to 83.17, at nearly twice the cost.

Oracle sentences and entities from the reference caption reach 94.27 CIDEr, so selection has room to improve. EAMA recalls the most reference entities, including 28.21% of NYTimes800k entities unseen in training, but a larger share of its generated names miss the reference than for Xu et al. (2024a).

demo.title: What each step adds, and how far the oracle is
demo.description: On NYTimes800k, the ablation adds one component at a time to InstructBLIP: full fine-tuning, then each alignment task, then the self-supplemented input. Table 4 adds the alternatives the paper tested: reading more of the article, and oracle sentences and entities taken from the reference caption. Switch the metric to see which steps help the caption scores and which help the named entities.
demo.note: Measured: all values from Tables 2 and 4 of arXiv 2402.19404v5 (NYTimes800k test set; BLEU-4, METEOR, ROUGE, CIDEr, and precision and recall of generated named entities). Computed: the change from the row named beside each value, and the share of the Base-to-oracle gap. Oracle rows use sentences and entities from the reference caption, which is unavailable at inference, so they are an upper bound rather than a method. The full-article model is trained and tested on the whole article, which the paper reports nearly doubles time and memory (Section 5.4). Single runs; no variance is reported.
